text: RACI is built for recurring activities. Some governance moments are different — genuinely contested, one-off decisions that need absolute clarity on who has the final say, named before the disagreement happens.

DACI — Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed — is lightweight, popularized by Atlassian, for everyday decisions. RAPID — Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide — from Bain and Company, is heavier, for bigger stakes. Both isolate one thing: exactly one person holds final say.

A policy exception needs a named Approver so it's not a fresh negotiation every time. A cross-domain dispute lands with the committee, but decision rights say who inside the committee breaks the tie. And when there's more work than capacity, someone has to Decide what gets attention first — with input, but without a veto from everyone else.

It feels more democratic to leave "who decides" vague until the moment arrives. In practice, that's when it turns personal — the fight becomes about who gets to decide, on top of the actual question. Naming it in advance keeps the real disagreement in focus.
That closes chapter two — policies, standards, workflows, issues, and decision rights. Chapter three turns to measuring whether all of this is actually working: governance KPIs.
